name: Tiratricol (Triac)
lead: Tiratricol, also called Triac or 3,3',5-triiodothyroacetic acid, is a synthetic thyroid hormone analogue and a metabolite of triiodothyronine (T3) that binds thyroid hormone receptors.[1][2][13] Taken by mouth, it was authorised in the European Union in February 2025 as Emcitate for peripheral thyrotoxicosis in people with MCT8 deficiency (Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome), and Egetis Therapeutics announced US approval of Emcitate in September 2026.[2][3][13][17]

Its place in appearance culture comes from a different history. Thyroid-active compounds raise metabolic activity, and around 2000 tiratricol, sold as Triacana or in Triax-type supplements, was discussed on bodybuilding forums as a way to reach lower body fat during a cutting phase, where leanness shows more muscle definition.[14][15][16] It was sold over the counter in fat-loss supplements in the early 2000s, and case reports from that period describe hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism and periodic paralysis in users.[4][5][6][7]

The research base is mostly about the medical indication. A phase 2 trial in MCT8 deficiency was published in 2019, 1990s randomised studies compared tiratricol with levothyroxine in people without thyroid glands, and a phase 3 withdrawal study has been registered.[1][9][10][12] The US label carries a boxed warning that thyroid hormones should not be used for obesity or weight loss, and no trial has tested tiratricol as a weight-loss or appearance treatment.[3]

paras: Tiratricol is an analogue of the thyroid hormone T3 in which the amino-acid side chain is replaced by an acetic acid group. It acts as a thyroid hormone receptor agonist and, unlike T3, can enter cells without the MCT8 transporter.[1][2][13] Wikipedia gives its formula as C14H9I3O4 and describes metabolism by glucuronidation in the liver with excretion through the bile.[2]

Thyroid hormones set the pace of the body's energy use, which is why thyroid-active substances attracted interest from people trying to lose fat. The US label for the approved product states in a boxed warning that thyroid hormones, including tiratricol, should not be used for the treatment of obesity or for weight loss.[3]

MCT8 deficiency, or Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome, is a rare X-linked disorder caused by mutations in the SLC16A2 gene. Thyroid hormone cannot enter brain cells properly, giving severe neurological disability, while circulating T3 is high and drives peripheral thyrotoxicosis with weight loss, tachycardia and muscle wasting.[1][2][17] The company's announcement describes a median life expectancy of about 35 years.[17]

A 2025 review in Drugs describes the milestones to tiratricol's first approval on 12 February 2025 in the EU, for peripheral thyrotoxicosis in MCT8 deficiency from birth, as 350 microgram dispersible tablets.[13] Wikipedia reports that the European medicines committee gave a positive opinion in December 2024, that in France tiratricol is also available for thyroid hormone resistance and as adjuvant therapy in thyroid cancer, and that the FDA granted orphan drug, rare pediatric disease, fast track, breakthrough therapy and priority review designations.[2]

Egetis Therapeutics, a Stockholm-based company, announced FDA approval of Emcitate for adults and children with MCT8 deficiency in a press release dated 28 September 2026. It lists the supporting programmes as ReTRIACt, Triac Trial I, Triac Trial II, two Erasmus Medical Center studies and a US expanded access programme.[17] The label says it is not recommended for primary hypothyroidism and is contraindicated in primary hyperthyroidism.[3][17]

Randomised studies in people without thyroid glands found tiratricol had stronger effects on liver and skeletal markers than on the pituitary when compared with levothyroxine, suggesting tissue-selective activity.[9][10] In the 1997 trial, 24 athyreotic patients were randomised to tiratricol or levothyroxine at doses that suppressed TSH equally; resting metabolic rate, weight and symptom score did not differ significantly between groups, while total and LDL cholesterol fell more with tiratricol and sex hormone-binding globulin rose by about 55 percent.[9]

The US label lists diarrhea, vomiting, rash and excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis) as the most common adverse reactions, and warns of thyrotoxicosis symptoms such as raised heart rate and insomnia during initiation and titration. It also notes that tiratricol can cause T3 immunoassays to read high.[3][17] Wikipedia also lists irritability, anxiety and nightmares.[2]

Tiratricol was studied as a thyroid hormone analogue in the early 1990s, including a 1992 randomised trial describing organ-specific effects in athyreotic patients.[10] It was marketed in Brazil, where its authorisation was suspended in 2003.[2] Its modern history as a medicine runs through MCT8 deficiency trials, a 2019 phase 2 report, an EU approval in February 2025 and a US approval announced in 2026.[1][13][17]

In the early 2000s tiratricol was sold in the United States over the counter as a thyroid-support or 'metabolic accelerator' fat-loss supplement. On T Nation in 2000, a member asked whether tiratricol (as Triacana) and the related products Triax, DNP and usnic acid were 'as bad as people say' or simply misused.[14] Replies in that thread were mixed: one user who tried a Triax-equivalent reported the fastest weight loss they had seen but said it did not distinguish fat from muscle and suppressed natural thyroid function, while others advised against it.[14]

Forum members in 2001 and 2002 asked about side effects and how to fit tiratricol around other cutting and recovery products, and cutting plans posted later listed it beside clenbuterol, ephedrine and liothyronine.[15][16][18][20] A 2001 poster said the company behind related products had never had safety 'its slightest concern'.[19] This wiki does not reproduce the dosing discussed in those threads.

Case reports describe symptomatic hyperthyroidism in an 87-year-old woman who took tiratricol among supplements recommended by her chiropractor,[5] hypothyroidism with lethargy and muscle weakness in two fit adults after several weeks of an over-the-counter fat-loss product,[6] thyroid dysfunction from over-the-counter use in Australia,[7] and hypokalemic thyrotoxic periodic paralysis in a 23-year-old bodybuilder who had used 'Triax Metabolic Accelerator' for about two months; his symptoms resolved with potassium and a beta-blocker.[4] Analytical work has also found tiratricol among adulterants in slimming capsules sold in Italy.[8]

Tiratricol is a prescription medicine where approved. Brazil suspended its marketing authorisation in 2003, and the EU and US approvals are limited to MCT8 deficiency.[2][13][17] The US label's boxed warning against use for obesity or weight loss applies to the approved product.[3]

An international, single-arm, open-label phase 2 trial in male children and adults with MCT8 deficiency across eight European countries and one South African site reported that Triac lowered the elevated T3 and addressed features of peripheral thyrotoxicosis such as tachycardia and weight loss.[1] Further registered trials include a phase 2 study in 22 patients,[11] a phase 3 withdrawal study in 20 males,[12] and a phase 2 trial of a topical gel with TRIAC and DHEA for glucocorticoid-induced skin atrophy.[21] The 1992 and 1997 randomised studies in athyreotic patients are described above.[9][10] No studies found of tiratricol for weight loss or cosmetic purposes.

lore.intro: Tiratricol, usually under the names Triacana, Triax or 'T2', appears in T Nation threads from the early 2000s as a supplement-era fat burner for cutting, alongside DNP, usnic acid, clenbuterol and ephedrine.[14][15][16]

claims.claim: Tiratricol is an effective fat burner for the end of a cut.
claims.believers: One 2000 poster reported it worked faster than any product they had tried, and cutting plans listed Triacana with clenbuterol, ephedrine and Cytomel.[14][16][18]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested tiratricol for weight loss, and the US label warns that thyroid hormones should not be used for obesity or weight loss.[3] In the 1997 randomised trial, weight and resting metabolic rate did not differ between tiratricol and levothyroxine at matched TSH suppression.[9]

claims.claim: It costs muscle and the fat comes back afterwards.
claims.believers: The same thread's users said it did not distinguish fat from muscle, that it suppressed natural thyroid function, and that some weight returned as the thyroid recovered; a 2002 poster asked whether tiratricol would 'eat muscle' after a cycle.[14][22]
claims.experts: Hypothyroidism after a short course of an over-the-counter tiratricol product has been reported in case reports, and no controlled study of body composition in healthy users exists.[6]

claims.claim: The risks come mainly from misuse.
claims.believers: A 2000 forum post asked whether tiratricol and related products are simply misused, abused and misunderstood.[14]
claims.experts: Case reports from supplement use describe hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism and periodic paralysis, including in a bodybuilder.[4][5][6][7]

claims.claim: Tiratricol hits the liver and fat selectively, so it is safer than T3.
claims.believers: Some posters treated its tissue-selective profile as an advantage over other thyroid hormones.[14]
claims.experts: The 1990s trials found stronger liver and bone effects than levothyroxine at matched TSH suppression, and the studied populations were people without thyroid glands, not healthy dieters.[9][10]

claims.believers: A 2001 poster said T-2 was far less TSH-suppressing than 'that tiratricol crap that used to be sold'.[23]
claims.experts: No published studies compare T2 products with tiratricol for fat loss.

card.summary: A thyroid-hormone analogue now approved for a rare genetic disorder, once sold as a fat-burner with case reports of thyroid dysfunction.
card.note: US label carries a boxed warning against use for obesity or weight loss.

quick.overview:
Tiratricol is a synthetic thyroid hormone analogue. It is approved for peripheral thyrotoxicosis in MCT8 deficiency, a rare genetic condition.

In the early 2000s it was sold in OTC fat-loss supplements. No trial has tested it for weight loss.
quick.mechanism: It activates thyroid hormone receptors and can enter cells without the MCT8 transporter.
quick.risks: Case reports describe hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism and periodic paralysis from supplement use. The label warns against use for obesity or weight loss.

chain: Used in cutting phases to reach lower body fat and a leaner look
angle.text: Bodybuilders on forums described tiratricol as a thyroid-type fat burner for the end of a diet, where lower body fat shows more muscle definition. Its approved use today is for a rare thyroid transport disorder.
